title: Two meanings of “quantum trading”
summary: A research programme and a scam share one name. Learn to tell them apart, then see where the course goes.

shots.title:
One word,
two worlds.
shots.subtitle: Search for **quantum trading** and you'll find serious research — and a scam.
shots.narration: Search for quantum trading and you will find two very different things. One is a serious research programme. The other is a scam.

left.heading: The research
items: Banks and labs test quantum algorithms on real data

shots.narration: On one side, banks and labs testing quantum algorithms and publishing their results with caveats. On the other, so-called Quantum AI bots, sold with fake celebrity videos.

shots.label: better predictions of whether a **bond quote would be filled** — HSBC and IBM, 2025
shots.context: A real, published trial. Relative gain, one bank's data.
shots.narration: Here is the research world. In 2025, HSBC and IBM reported up to 34 percent better predictions of whether a bond quote would be filled, using quantum processors. A trial — but real.

shots.text: Australia's regulator called “Quantum AI” the **most prolific** trading-platform scam it had seen.
shots.footnote: ASIC, 2024. The UK FCA lists it as an unauthorised firm.
shots.narration: And here is the other world. Australia's securities regulator named Quantum AI the most prolific online trading-platform scam it had seen. Britain's regulator lists it as unauthorised.

shots.heading: The scam playbook
items: A celebrity “endorses” it in a video
shots.narration: The scam follows a script: a celebrity video, a small first deposit of around two hundred and fifty dollars, a dashboard showing fake profits, pressure to add more, and then withdrawals that never arrive.

shots.text: No quantum computer today can run a trading strategy that **guarantees** returns. Anyone who says so is selling something.
shots.narration: So here is your first filter. No quantum computer today can run a trading strategy that guarantees returns. Anyone telling you otherwise is selling something.

nodes.label: Your brief for a trading desk

shots.narration: This course takes the research seriously. We start with just enough theory, then build working labs for pricing and portfolios, map what has actually been shown, and finish with a brief you could hand to a trading desk.

shots.text: Every claim in this course has a **source** and a **date**. Look in the margin.
shots.narration: One more thing. Every factual claim in this course is checked against its source and dated. When you see a number, look in the margin: the evidence is right there.

steps.title: Research or red flag?
steps.brief: Sort each statement. Some are real, published results; others are the language of scams. Pick a card, then a bucket.

cards.text: A bank reports up to 34% better fill-probability predictions in a bond-trading trial with IBM.
cards.why: HSBC and IBM published this in 2025 — as a trial, with a preprint and caveats.

cards.text: Our quantum AI bot made members 90% in a week. Start with just $250!
cards.why: Guaranteed-sounding returns plus a small starter deposit is the exact script regulators describe.

cards.text: Researchers ran a certified-randomness protocol on a 56-qubit quantum computer and published it in Nature.
A famous billionaire explains in a video why he moved his savings into a quantum trading app.
cards.why: Deepfake celebrity endorsements are the scam's main advertising channel.

cards.text: Your dashboard shows big profits, but you must pay a ‘release fee’ before withdrawing.
cards.why: Fake dashboards and blocked withdrawals are named warning signs.

cards.text: A study estimates useful quantum advantage in derivative pricing needs thousands of error-corrected qubits.
cards.why: Goldman Sachs and IBM published this resource estimate in 2021 — research is often about what is not yet possible.

questions.prompt: Which describes the HSBC–IBM bond result most accurately?
options: A production trading system that beats all classical methods
A published trial showing up to 34% better fill predictions on one bank's data
questions.explain: HSBC described it as a trial. The gain is relative and measured on its own historical data.

questions.prompt: Which of these are warning signs regulators list for investment-platform scams?
questions.explain: Fake endorsements, pressure to top up and blocked withdrawals all appear in ASIC's warning.

questions.prompt: Can a quantum computer today run a strategy that guarantees trading profits?
options: No — and claims that it can are a red flag
questions.explain: Even the leading bank results are exploratory trials, not guaranteed-return systems.
